The detail that breaks the usual reassurances: the agents ran the attacker's code even when explicitly told to ignore it, and endpoint detection, firewalls, and prompt-level guardrails all missed it. The standard mitigation story for prompt injection has been some version of "instruct the model not to comply," and this is a clean demonstration that the instruction does not hold when the malicious input arrives dressed as trusted tool output.

This is the structural tension in agentic tooling. The autonomy that lets an agent read your errors and fix them is the same autonomy that lets injected instructions act on your machine, and every MCP connection widens the set of places that poison can come from. Treating tool output as trusted is the bug, and right now most setups do exactly that.

If you run coding agents against real systems, scope their permissions hard, sandbox anything they execute, and stop letting them auto-run proposed commands against production. The safe default is to treat everything an agent reads from an external source as untrusted input, including the error reports it was built to help with.

item.title: Police Seize AudiA6, the Mixer That Washed $380M for Ransomware Crews
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: An international operation led by Europol and the US DOJ dismantled AudiA6, a crypto-laundering service that cleaned more than $380 million for ransomware gangs and arrested two of its alleged operators in Georgia.
item.content:encoded:
A service that promised to launder dirty cryptocurrency and return it clean in about an hour, for a cut of 3 to 10 percent, is offline. Two of its alleged operators are now in custody in Georgia.

The takedown of AudiA6 came on June 10, run jointly by the US Department of Justice, the Secret Service, and Europol. Investigators say the platform operated as a central laundering hub from 2022 to 2025 and moved more than $380 million, roughly 336 million euros, for criminal clients. The coordinated action seized 25 domains, pulled more than 30 servers offline, confiscated over 80 vehicles and several properties in Georgia, and froze around 692,000 euros in crypto. The two administrators arrested hold Ukrainian and Russian nationality.

Ransomware gets the headlines, but cashing out is the part that actually constrains it. Encrypting a hospital is easy. Turning the ransom into spendable money without getting traced is the hard problem, and services like AudiA6 are the plumbing that solves it. Europol says the operation has been linked to more than 15 separate ransomware investigations, which is the real measure of what just got disrupted.

Worth being clear-eyed about what this does and does not accomplish. Domain seizures are reversible, and mixer operators rebrand and resurface with depressing regularity. What raises the cost is the arrests and the asset seizures, the part where running this business stops being anonymous and starts being a prison sentence. That is the difference between knocking over a storefront and actually deterring the trade.

For defenders, the takeaway is less about any single service and more about the pressure on the cash-out layer. Every laundering pipeline that gets dismantled makes the economics of ransomware a little worse, which is slow, unglamorous progress, and the only kind that lasts.

item.title: Google Patches a Chrome V8 Zero-Day That's Already Being Exploited
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Chrome 149.0.7827.102 fixes CVE-2026-11645, an actively exploited out-of-bounds bug in the V8 engine that lets a malicious web page run code inside the browser sandbox.
item.content:encoded:
Every Chrome user has an update waiting, and this one is not optional. Google pushed a fix on June 8 for CVE-2026-11645, a flaw in V8 that attackers are already using against real targets.

V8 is the engine that runs JavaScript and WebAssembly on every page Chrome loads, which is what makes a bug here serious. This one is an out-of-bounds memory access rated 8.8, and a crafted HTML page is enough to trigger code execution inside the browser sandbox. A user does not have to download anything. Visiting the wrong page is the whole exploit.

The flaw was reported on April 27 by a researcher credited as 303f06e3, who collected a $55,000 bounty for it. That leaves a gap of roughly six weeks between the report and the public fix, which is normal for a complex engine bug but worth noticing given that exploitation was happening in that window. The patch ships in Chrome 149.0.7827.102 and .103 for Windows and macOS, and .102 for Linux.

Google is holding back the technical detail on the exploit until most users have updated, which is standard practice and also a tell that the bug is being used in ways the team does not want to advertise. A sandbox-contained flaw is not full system compromise on its own, but these rarely travel alone. They get chained with a sandbox escape, and then it is a different conversation. CISA added the CVE to its exploited-vulnerabilities catalog on June 9.

The action here is boring and immediate. Open your version page, confirm you are on 149.0.7827.102 or later, and restart the browser to apply it. If you manage a fleet, push the update through policy rather than trusting users to relaunch on their own.

item.title: Check Point VPN Zero-Day Under Attack Since May, Now in CISA's KEV
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-50751, a 9.3-rated authentication bypass in Check Point's Remote Access VPN, has been exploited since early May, with at least one intrusion tied to a Qilin ransomware affiliate.
item.content:encoded:
An attacker can open a VPN session into a Check Point gateway without a valid password. That is the whole problem with CVE-2026-50751, and it has been happening in the wild since May 7.

The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.3 and is classified as improper authentication. It lives in the IKEv1 key-exchange logic, and it lets an unauthenticated attacker establish a session as though they had legitimate credentials. It affects Remote Access VPN, Mobile Access, and the Spark Firewall line across nine version branches, from R80.20.x up through R82.10. If you run a Check Point gateway exposed to the internet, the odds are good you are in scope.

Rapid7's researchers confirmed two intrusions with high confidence and tied at least one of them, with medium confidence, to an affiliate of the Qilin ransomware operation. Check Point's own framing calls the campaign limited, several dozen organizations so far. That number is doing a lot of work. A perimeter VPN that hands out authenticated sessions is exactly the front door a ransomware crew wants, and "several dozen" is a snapshot, not a ceiling. Once a reliable exploit circulates, limited campaigns stop being limited.

Check Point has shipped hotfixes, and CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in early June with a federal remediation deadline attached. That KEV listing is the part defenders should read as a clock, not a footnote: it means the government has seen enough real exploitation to compel agencies to patch.

If you operate these gateways, apply the hotfix now and treat any internet-facing instance as potentially already touched. Hunt for VPN sessions you cannot account for, new or unexpected administrative activity, and the usual post-access tradecraft that precedes a ransomware deployment. Patching closes the door. It does not tell you whether someone already walked through it.

item.title: KKR and Nvidia Put $10B Into a Company to Fix Stalled AI Data Centers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: KKR, Nvidia, Vistra, and Kuwait's sovereign fund launched Helix Digital Infrastructure with more than $10 billion to build the power and data centers hyperscalers keep announcing but failing to deliver.
item.content:encoded:
There's a gap between the data centers companies announce and the ones that actually come online. KKR just put more than $10 billion behind closing it.

On June 11, KKR, Nvidia, Vistra, and the Kuwait Investment Authority launched Helix Digital Infrastructure, a company built to finance and deliver AI infrastructure for hyperscale customers. The pitch is integration: bundle data center capacity, power, connectivity, and the services around them into one package, instead of making a hyperscaler stitch those pieces together itself. Nvidia comes in as the strategic technology partner, and Vistra as the preferred power supplier.

Running it is Adam Selipsky, who used to be CEO of Amazon Web Services. He isn't pretending the buildout is going smoothly. By his account, more than a quarter of announced data center projects aren't getting delivered, and Helix exists to attack that delivery gap rather than to add another splashy capacity number to the pile.

Selipsky's point about undelivered projects is the honest part of an otherwise familiar story. The constraint on AI infrastructure stopped being chips a while ago and became power, permits, and the ability to actually finish construction. Money keeps pouring in regardless. KKR's $10 billion lands the same week Amazon reportedly lined up $17.5 billion in bank loans and Google signed a compute deal with SpaceX worth about $920 million a month. A lot of capital is chasing the same scarce megawatts.

For everyone who isn't a hyperscaler, this is the plumbing of the AI boom getting financialized. Whether Helix delivers faster than the projects Selipsky is criticizing is the thing to watch. The capital is clearly available. Turning it into powered, online racks is the part that keeps slipping.

item.title: Is Security+ Worth It in 2026? An Honest Look at the SY0-701
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Security+ is the most-requested entry cybersecurity cert and a DoD baseline requirement, but it opens doors rather than handing you a six-figure analyst salary on day one.
item.content:encoded:
Security+ is the cert that gets oversold in both directions. One camp treats it as a golden ticket into a $125,000 security analyst job. The other dismisses it as a memorization test that proves nothing. Both are wrong, and the truth in between is genuinely good news: Security+ is the single most reliable way to get past a hiring filter for an entry-level security role, and that's a meaningful thing to buy for a few hundred dollars.

The current exam is SY0-701, and it's been the only active version since CompTIA retired SY0-601 in July 2024. It runs up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, including performance-based questions, and you need 750 out of 900 to pass. Retail pricing in the US sits around $425 for a single voucher. There's no formal prerequisite, though CompTIA suggests Network+ and a couple of years of IT experience first, and that background genuinely makes the exam easier.

The content is organized into five domains: General Security Concepts (12%), Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%), Security Architecture (18%), Security Operations (28%), and Security Program Management and Oversight (20%). The weighting toward operations and threats reflects what the cert is really for: showing you can function in a SOC or a security-adjacent IT role, not that you can write policy from scratch.

Now the salary question, handled honestly. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a 2024 median wage of $124,910 for information security analysts, with employment projected to grow 29% through 2034 and roughly 16,000 openings a year. That growth is real and it's why the cert is in demand. But that median reflects experienced analysts, not someone who just passed Security+. A fresh Security+ holder is typically looking at the bottom of that range or a notch below it, in roles like junior SOC analyst, security administrator, or an IT job with security duties. The cert points you up that ladder; it doesn't teleport you to the top of it.

There's one advantage that's easy to undersell: Security+ is an approved baseline certification under the US Department of Defense's workforce requirements (DoD 8140/8570). For a large set of government and defense-contractor roles, holding it isn't a nice-to-have, it's a checkbox you cannot be hired without. If that's the world you're aiming at, the worth-it question is already answered.

How hard is it? Moderate, and the difficulty is specific. The volume of terminology is large, and the performance-based questions reward people who've actually configured something over people who've only read about it. The other trap is CompTIA's question style, which loves asking for the "best" answer among several that are all defensible. Knowing the definition isn't enough; you have to know which control fits which scenario.

Which points at how to study. Professor Messer's free SY0-701 series remains the backbone most people build on, paired with a paid course if you want structure. But the candidates who pass on the first try are the ones who drill performance-based scenarios and run a question bank hard enough to expose the gap between "I recognize this term" and "I know when to use it." Hands-on practice and realistic question reps are what close that gap, far more than rereading a study guide. For an entry security cert in 2026, Security+ is worth it. Just buy it for what it is: the door, not the room.

item.title: Microsoft Built Its Own Frontier Models. The Target Is OpenAI's Bill.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft's seven new in-house MAI models, led by the reasoning model MAI-Thinking-1, are built to run on Azure without licensing fees, and the strategy matters more than the benchmarks.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft spent years reselling OpenAI's models as its own AI products. At Build this month it showed the alternative it's been building quietly: seven models trained in-house, headlined by MAI-Thinking-1, its first reasoning model.

MAI-Thinking-1 is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with about 35 billion active parameters out of roughly a trillion total, and a 256,000-token context window. Microsoft says it was trained on commercially licensed data with no distillation from third-party models, OpenAI's included. Alongside it: MAI-Code-1-Flash, a small 5-billion-parameter coding model headed into VS Code and GitHub Copilot, plus image, transcription, and voice models.

The benchmark line Microsoft is pushing is that in blind human comparisons MAI-Thinking-1 was preferred over Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 and held its own against Claude Opus 4.6 on SWE Bench Pro coding tasks. Take that the way you take any vendor's own evals: directionally interesting, not independent proof. "Preferred in blind tests we ran" is a claim, not a leaderboard.

The benchmarks aren't the point anyway. The point is the bill. Every time Microsoft serves an OpenAI model, it pays for that model. Running its own models on Azure cuts the royalty out, and Satya Nadella framed the shift as moving from "consuming a frontier model to fully participating at the frontier." For developers, the promised payoff is lower per-token pricing. For Microsoft, it's options in a partnership that has grown lopsided, and room to negotiate the next OpenAI deal from a stronger position.

None of this means Microsoft is dropping OpenAI. GPT models still sit at the center of Copilot, and Microsoft has every reason to keep that relationship going. But a company that can credibly run its own frontier-class models is a different kind of partner than one that can't. That's the message Build was really sending.

item.title: Is the AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03) Worth It?
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The SAA-C03 is the most-requested cloud cert in job postings, but it rewards people who already know AWS and quietly punishes those treating it as a first step.
item.content:encoded:
The AWS Solutions Architect Associate is the cloud cert that shows up most in job postings, and that alone makes it worth taking seriously. But there's a trap baked into how people approach it. They see "associate" in the name and assume it's a beginner cert. It isn't. The SAA-C03 assumes you already understand how AWS services fit together, and it tests your judgment about which one to reach for, not whether you can define them.

The exam specifics: 65 questions in 130 minutes, of which 50 are scored and 15 are unscored items AWS uses to trial future questions. You need a scaled score of 720 out of 1,000 to pass, and it costs $150 in the US. There's no hard prerequisite, but AWS recommends about a year of hands-on experience, and that recommendation is doing more work than it looks.

Four domains, and the weighting tells the story: Design Secure Architectures (30%), Design Resilient Architectures (26%), Design High-Performing Architectures (24%), and Design Cost-Optimized Architectures (20%). Every domain is the word "design." That's the whole exam in one observation. You're not being asked what S3 is. You're being asked, given a scenario with latency targets, a budget, and a compliance constraint, which storage class and which architecture you'd choose. The questions are little case studies, often two or three plausible-looking answers deep.

That design framing is also why it's harder than the question count suggests. Two answers will usually be technically correct and one will be the right call for the scenario's actual priority, whether that's cost, durability, or recovery time. You can't pattern-match your way through that. You have to genuinely understand the tradeoffs between, say, Multi-AZ and read replicas, or when a NAT gateway beats a NAT instance. This is where pure flashcard study falls apart.

The payoff is real and it's the strongest of any cert in this group. The SAA shows up in a large share of cloud job listings, and aggregated salary data from sites like ZipRecruiter and Glassdoor puts cloud roles tied to it well into six figures, commonly in the $140,000-plus range for people with a couple of years of experience. Those are aggregator numbers rather than a government statistic, so read them as the shape of the market, not a guarantee. The direction is not in doubt: cloud architecture pays, and this cert is the recognized entry ticket.

Here's the honest catch for career-changers. If you have zero AWS exposure, going straight for the SAA is a slog, and many people would be better served starting with the Cloud Practitioner to build vocabulary first, then coming back. The fastest path through the SAA for anyone runs through the console: spin up the services the exam covers, break them, watch the bill, see what fails over and what doesn't. Pair that with scenario-style practice questions in the weeks before the exam, because the test's whole personality is scenarios, and reading documentation does not prepare you for the judgment calls the way actually building does.

Worth it? For anyone serious about cloud work, yes, clearly. Just go in with the right expectation: this is a cert that confirms experience rather than substitutes for it. Earn it after you've put your hands on AWS, not before, and it does exactly what you want a cert to do.

item.title: Attackers Are Exploiting a Netlogon Bug That Owns Domain Controllers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-41089, a 9.8-rated unauthenticated Netlogon flaw Microsoft patched in May, is now under active exploitation against domain controllers, and Belgium's cyber agency is sounding louder alarms than Redmond.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft patched it in May. Attackers are using it now. CVE-2026-41089 is a critical hole in the Windows Netlogon service, and the gap between the fix and the exploitation is exactly where unpatched domain controllers live.

The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in how Netlogon handles inbound RPC requests. A crafted packet with a malformed length field writes past the buffer and overwrites the return address on the stack. Because the Netlogon RPC interface is exposed on every domain controller by design, no authentication is needed to reach the vulnerable code. It carries a 9.8 CVSS score and affects Windows Server from 2012 through 2025.

Successful exploitation runs code inside the LSASS process on a domain controller. In practical terms, that's the whole Active Directory forest. Whoever lands this owns the directory that authenticates everything else.

What makes this one notable is who's doing the warning. Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity confirmed active exploitation on June 1 and told organizations to treat it as an emergency, roughly three weeks after Microsoft's May Patch Tuesday shipped the fix. The CCB's messaging has been blunter and more urgent than Microsoft's own, and there's been visible friction between the two over how the bug was communicated. When a national CSIRT is shouting louder than the vendor, that tells you how seriously to take it.

If your domain controllers aren't on the May 2026 cumulative update, that's the job for today. Netlogon RPC can't simply be firewalled off internally without breaking authentication, so patching is the real fix, not network controls. Confirm every DC is current, and review logs for unusual Netlogon RPC traffic and LSASS crashes that could mark a failed exploit attempt.

item.title: Network+ in 2026: Is It Worth It and How Hard Is the N10-009?
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Network+ sits in an awkward spot between A+ and CCNA, so the real question is whether the N10-009 earns a place in your path or whether you should jump to Cisco instead.
item.content:encoded:
Network+ has an identity problem, and pretending otherwise does no one any favors. It's vendor-neutral networking knowledge that nobody disputes is useful, sitting directly underneath Cisco's CCNA, which carries more weight with employers and costs about the same. So the honest framing for 2026 isn't "is Network+ good" (it is) but "is Network+ the right next step for you, or are you about to pay for a cert you'll outgrow in a year?"

Here are the facts on the current exam. The code is N10-009, and it replaced N10-008 when that retired in December 2024. It runs up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, mixing multiple choice with performance-based questions, and you need 720 out of 900 to pass. The retail price is $369 in the US. CompTIA recommends A+ first plus around nine to twelve months of hands-on networking experience, though plenty of people sit it earlier than that.

The exam splits into five domains: Networking Fundamentals (23%), Network Implementations (20%), Network Operations (19%), Network Security (14%), and Network Troubleshooting (24%). Note where the weight sits. Troubleshooting and fundamentals together are nearly half the exam, and that tells you what CompTIA is actually testing: not whether you can recite the OSI model, but whether you can reason through why a host can't reach a server.

How hard is it? Harder than A+, easier than CCNA. The conceptual load is real this time. Subnetting alone defeats more candidates than anything else on the exam, and you cannot fake your way through it. If binary math and CIDR notation make your eyes glaze, that's the wall you have to climb before you sit this. The good news is that subnetting is a learnable mechanical skill, not a talent, and a week of deliberate practice gets most people from lost to fluent.

Where Network+ pays off is the role it points at. The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the 2024 median for network and computer systems administrators around $97,000, well above the help desk tier A+ targets. Network+ is the credential that signals you're ready to step from support into administration. It's also DoD-approved for certain baseline roles, which matters if you're aiming at government or contractor work.

The study reality mirrors the exam's troubleshooting bias. Reading about VLANs and routing teaches you the words; configuring them teaches you the cert. The candidates who pass cleanly are the ones who spend real time in a lab simulating the networks they're being tested on, then drill a question bank to surface the subnetting and port-number gaps they didn't know they had. Theory-only studiers consistently underestimate the performance-based questions and pay for it on test day.

So: worth it, with a caveat. If you want vendor-neutral fundamentals or you need the DoD approval, Network+ is a clean, defensible choice. If your goal is squarely network engineering and you're comfortable committing, the CCNA covers similar ground with more market pull for the same money, and you can skip a step. Network+ is the safer, broader bet. CCNA is the more ambitious one. Neither is wrong; just be honest with yourself about which you're making.

item.title: A Perfect-10 Ivanti Sentry Bug Is Already Backdooring Gateways
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-10520, an unauthenticated command-injection flaw in Ivanti Sentry rated a maximum 10.0, is under active exploitation, and CISA gave federal agencies until June 14 to patch.
item.content:encoded:
A CVSS score of 10.0 is rare. Ivanti Sentry just earned one, and attackers were on it within a day.

Ivanti's June 9 advisory covers two bugs. CVE-2026-10520 is an OS command injection flaw that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker run code as root, and it sits at the maximum 10.0 severity. The second, CVE-2026-10523, is an authentication bypass at 9.9 that lets an attacker create their own admin accounts. Either one alone is bad. Chained, they hand over the box.

Sentry is the gateway that brokers access between mobile devices and an organization's internal mail and app servers, so it's exposed on purpose and it sits in a trusted spot on the network. That's the worst combination for a pre-auth root flaw. Affected versions are 10.5.1, 10.6.1, 10.7.0 and earlier; the fixes are in 10.5.2, 10.6.2, and 10.7.1.

This isn't theoretical. After watchTowr published a proof-of-concept, the Shadowserver Foundation started seeing exploitation attempts and confirmed backdoored gateways within 24 hours. CISA added CVE-2026-10520 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal civilian agencies just three days to patch, with a deadline of June 14.

Three days is CISA's way of saying this is on fire. Patch to the fixed releases now. If your Sentry was internet-facing and unpatched at any point this week, don't just patch and move on. Assume compromise, look for new admin accounts and unexpected processes running as root, and rotate any credentials that gateway could reach.

item.title: Is CompTIA A+ Worth It in 2026? An Honest Look at the 220-1201 and 1202
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A+ is two exams, real money, and a slow on-ramp into IT, so here's who it actually pays off for and who should skip straight past it.
item.content:encoded:
A+ is the cert people argue about most, and the argument is usually framed wrong. The question isn't whether A+ is respected (it's fine) or whether it's hard (it isn't, really). The question is whether you're the person it's built for. If you've never held an IT job and need something on your resume that says you can fix a laptop and not break the network, A+ does that job better than anything else. If you already work a help desk, it's mostly a box to check for HR.

The current version is two exams, not one. Core 1 (220-1201) and Core 2 (220-1202) both launched in March 2025 and replaced the older 1101/1102 pair, which CompTIA retired in September 2025. You need to pass both to earn the cert. Each exam runs up to 90 questions in 90 minutes. Core 1 wants 675 out of 900 to pass; Core 2 wants 700. Core 1 covers hardware, networking basics, mobile devices, and virtualization and cloud concepts. Core 2 is the software half: operating systems, security fundamentals, troubleshooting, and operational procedures.

Now the part nobody likes. At CompTIA's retail pricing each exam runs around $250 in the US, so you're looking at roughly $500 to sit both, before any study materials. That's the real sticker shock of A+, and it's worth saying plainly: this is the most expensive entry-level cert relative to the salary it points you toward.

Because where A+ lands you is the entry of the entry level. The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the 2024 median wage for computer user support specialists around $60,000 and computer network support specialists around $73,000. A+ is the credential that gets you in the door for the first of those, the help desk and desktop support roles where you'll spend a year or two before moving up. Treat it as a starting line, not a destination.

How hard is it? The content is broad rather than deep. There's a lot of it (printers, RAM types, Windows recovery, common malware, cable standards) but very little of it is conceptually difficult. The thing that trips people up is breadth plus the performance-based questions, where you have to actually do something in a simulated environment rather than pick an answer. People who only memorize acronyms get wrecked by those. People who've physically opened a machine and clicked around an OS sail through them.

That's the honest study advice for A+: stop reading and start touching things. Build a cheap PC or tear down an old one. Run a Windows install in a VM, break it, fix it. The candidates who pass comfortably are the ones who pair a video course with real hands-on reps and a question bank to find their weak spots before exam day, not the ones who read a 1,200-page book cover to cover. The terminology sticks far better once you've watched it happen in front of you.

So is it worth it in 2026? If you're switching careers into IT with nothing else to show, yes, and pairing it with Network+ or Security+ within the year is the move that actually changes your pay. If you already have a year of help desk under your belt, your time and money are better spent skipping ahead. A+ proves you can start. It was never meant to prove more than that.

item.title: ShinyHunters Hit 100+ Orgs Through an Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle's out-of-band alert for CVE-2026-35273, a 9.8-rated unauthenticated RCE in PeopleSoft PeopleTools, lands after ShinyHunters had already used it to breach more than 100 organizations, most of them universities.
item.content:encoded:
More than a hundred organizations got breached before the vendor said a word. That's the shape of the Oracle PeopleSoft attack that came to light this week.

On June 10 Oracle put out an out-of-band Security Alert for CVE-2026-35273, a flaw in PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62. It's rated 9.8 on the CVSS scale: remote code execution, no authentication, no user interaction. An attacker who can reach the server over HTTP can run code on it. Because the attacks started before the alert went out, this was a true zero-day.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant tied the campaign to UNC6240, the crew that operates under the ShinyHunters name. They tracked the activity between May 27 and June 9, and the stolen data started showing up on the group's leak site on June 9. By the attackers' own count the campaign hit more than 100 organizations. Sixty-eight percent of the victims were in higher education, most of them in the United States.

The tradecraft is worth a look. The attackers stood up MeshCentral remote-management servers dressed up to look like legitimate cloud endpoints, registered a lookalike domain, and pushed a custom script to spread across networks and deface systems. This wasn't a smash-and-grab. It was a staged extortion operation that treated PeopleSoft as the front door to HR and student records.

There's a catch buried in Oracle's response. The alert points customers to a patch document, but that document sits behind a support login, so it isn't obvious to outsiders whether a full fix is even shipping yet. Oracle's headline guidance is mitigation: disable the Environment Management Hub service, or remove the PSEMHUB application entirely on single-server setups. Telling customers to rip out a component is not the same as handing them a patch.

If you run PeopleSoft, treat any internet-facing instance as suspect. Apply Oracle's mitigations now, hunt for unfamiliar MeshCentral agents and outbound connections to odd domains, and assume the EMHub component is the path attackers will try first. Education IT teams especially should check today, because that's where the attackers spent most of their time.

item.title: CompTIA CySA+ V4 Lands June 23: Sit the Old Exam or Wait?
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CompTIA's analyst cert gets a refresh on June 23 with new AI governance, cloud, and threat-hunting content, and if you're mid-prep you have a real decision to make.
item.content:encoded:
If you're studying for CySA+ right now, you've got a decision to make: sit the current exam before it ages out, or wait for the new one.

CompTIA launches CySA+ V4, exam code CS0-004, on June 23. The current version, CS0-003, stays available for a while after that. CompTIA usually runs about six months of overlap before retiring an old exam, though it hasn't put a firm retirement date on CS0-003 yet. Both versions carry the same name and certify the same thing; only the objectives differ.

V4 keeps the four-domain structure but reweights and modernizes it. The domains are Security Operations (34%), Vulnerability Management (26%), Incident Response and Management (24%), and Reporting and Communication (16%). The new material is where the cert catches up to the actual job: more cloud, a real emphasis on threat hunting, expanded identity and access management, and a fresh block on AI use cases, the risks they bring, and governance. Format is up to 85 questions in 165 minutes, with a passing score of 750 on a 100-to-900 scale.

Here's the practical call. If you're within a few weeks of testing and your material is built around CS0-003, finish what you started and sit the current exam. There's no penalty for holding a cert earned on the older objectives; it's the same credential on your resume. If you're earlier in your prep, or you work somewhere cloud-heavy or AI-adjacent, the V4 objectives map better to what you'll actually be doing, and that's worth waiting a few weeks for.

CySA+ is CompTIA's analyst cert, a step past Security+ and aimed at people doing detection, triage, and response rather than general security awareness. The V4 additions push it toward the SOC reality of 2026: cloud telemetry, hunting instead of waiting on alerts, and working out what to do when half your tooling suddenly has an AI feature bolted on. If that's the chair you sit in, or want to, the refresh is aimed at you.

One thing not to overthink, but to plan around: test-prep churn. New exam versions always arrive before the third-party practice questions and courses fully catch up. If you go for CS0-004 in its first month, lean on CompTIA's own objectives document over a hastily updated cram deck, and expect the AI and cloud sections to be the thinnest part of any third-party prep until the market fills them in.

item.title: OpenAI Models Are Coming to Oracle Cloud's Prepaid Credits
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle Cloud customers will soon be able to spend their existing Universal Credits on OpenAI's models and Codex, turning a procurement headache into a budgeting line item.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI wants to sell its models to companies that never signed up for OpenAI. Its new deal with Oracle is how.

Under the partnership, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure customers will be able to spend their existing Oracle Universal Credits, the prepaid cloud commitments many enterprises already buy in bulk, on OpenAI's frontier models and its Codex coding agent. The models will be offered through the OCI Marketplace, and OpenAI says access arrives in the coming weeks.

There's no new model here and no new capability. What's new is the procurement path. For a large company, the friction in adopting OpenAI usually isn't technical; it's the legal and purchasing overhead of onboarding another vendor. Letting teams draw down a cloud commitment they already signed off on removes a step that quietly kills plenty of pilots before they start.

The two companies are already deep in business together. Oracle is one of the main compute providers behind OpenAI's data-center buildout, the Stargate effort, so wiring OpenAI's models into Oracle's marketplace is the customer-facing other half of an infrastructure deal that was mostly about who rents whom servers. This turns that plumbing into a sales channel.

It also tightens the knot. Every credit an Oracle customer spends on GPT through OCI is a credit they don't spend on a competing model, and it deepens the dependency between one cloud and one model vendor. Convenient for buyers today, and worth remembering the next time someone argues the AI market is still wide open.

For engineers the practical read is simple. If your shop runs on Oracle Cloud, getting GPT-class models and Codex into a project is about to be a budgeting question instead of a procurement project. That's a smaller change than a new model, and for a lot of teams it will matter more.

item.title: CISA: Patch the Actively Exploited SolarWinds Serv-U Flaw by June 19
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-28318 lets an unauthenticated attacker crash SolarWinds Serv-U with a single crafted POST request, and CISA has set a June 19 deadline to fix it.
item.content:encoded:
SolarWinds is back on CISA's exploited-vulnerabilities list, this time for a flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker knock its Serv-U file-transfer server offline with a single crafted request.

CVE-2026-28318 is an uncontrolled resource consumption bug. A remote attacker with no credentials can trigger it by sending an HTTP POST request carrying a Content-Encoding: deflate header, which forces Serv-U to chew through resources until the service crashes. Every version up to and including 15.5.4 is affected. SolarWinds fixed it in Serv-U 15.5.4 Hotfix 1.

It's a denial-of-service bug, not remote code execution, so nobody is stealing files through this one directly. But Serv-U is managed file-transfer software, the kind of appliance that sits at the edge of a network moving sensitive data between partners. Knocking it down on demand is disruptive on its own, and DoS against file-transfer gear has a habit of being either a precursor or a distraction.

CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 5 and gave federal civilian agencies until June 19 to patch. That window is nearly shut. A KEV listing isn't theoretical: CISA only adds bugs it has evidence are being used in real attacks.

Serv-U has been here before. The same product showed up in CISA's catalog for a path-traversal flaw in 2024 and a remote-code-execution bug in 2021 that was tied to state-linked activity. For software whose entire job is to sit exposed and move files, that's a track record worth weighing when you decide how fast to act.

If you run Serv-U, get to 15.5.4 Hotfix 1. If you can't patch right away, SolarWinds and CISA point to the same stopgaps: put the service behind a WAF or firewall so only known addresses can reach it, and block POST requests that include a content-encoding header. Neither is a real substitute for the fix.
